what_the_class_is: The two-voice pitch shifter as a whole: two shifters off the mono sum of the inputs, each behind its own pre-delay and placed by its own EFX Pan byte, weighed against each other by L.Bal, mixed with the dry by the balance byte, then the level and tone stages.

era.when: Mid nineteen-nineties, a custom fixed-point DSP running its effects at 32 kHz with a small control processor beside it.
what_that_implies: A time-domain shifter is a circular buffer read by pointers that move through it at the ratio and jump back by a stored length when they reach the end of it; two pointers a length apart, crossfaded, hide the jump. It costs two interpolated reads and a few multiplies a sample and no transform.
The length is a table the mode byte indexes, and a table whose entries are powers of two costs nothing to wrap: the pointer arithmetic is a mask.
A feedback shifter writes its own output back into what it reads, so each pass through the loop is shifted again and the repeats climb or fall by the ratio.
Times, levels and corners are tables indexed by the byte, as the classes that read them closed on; a whole-type model borrows those tables rather than fitting its own.
era.would_be_wrong_if: The splice rate at settings nothing here was built on came back other than the ratio's distance from one over the window the mode byte picks, or a copy of the output in itself stood at a distance that does not follow the mode byte.

candidates.reading: Each pitch byte is a shifter whose window is the one the mode byte picks over the ratio's distance from one, so the read-out drifts a window at a time and is re-entered there. The pair stored a whole window apart, and a straight crossfade between the two read-outs.
candidates.predicts: Splices at the ratio's distance from one over the window, and a copy of the output in itself a whole window apart in what is stored; the level dips at every splice for as long as the straight fade takes to cross.

candidates.reading: Each pitch byte is a shifter whose window is the one the mode byte picks over the ratio's distance from one, so the read-out drifts a window at a time and is re-entered there. The pair stored a whole window apart, and a raised-cosine crossfade between the two read-outs.
candidates.predicts: Splices at the ratio's distance from one over the window, and a copy of the output in itself a whole window apart in what is stored; the level dips at every splice and is back sooner than under a straight fade.

candidates.reading: Each pitch byte is a shifter whose window is the one the mode byte picks over the ratio's distance from one, so the read-out drifts a window at a time and is re-entered there. The pair stored half a window apart, and a straight crossfade between the two read-outs.
candidates.predicts: Splices twice as often as the window claim reads, and a copy half a window apart in what is stored, which at the octave arrives a quarter window apart.

candidates.reading: Each pitch byte is a shifter whose window is the one the mode byte picks over the ratio's distance from one, so the read-out drifts a window at a time and is re-entered there. The pair stored half a window apart, and a raised-cosine crossfade between the two read-outs.
candidates.predicts: Splices twice as often as the window claim reads, and a copy half a window apart in what is stored; the raised-cosine fade shortens each dip.

what_no_candidate_here_predicts: The copy a window apart at unison. At a ratio of one the node's sweep is nothing and both pointers read the same place, so every candidate returns the input a sample late where the unit holds a copy of it a window back.

What coarse and fine do together. Each is its own shifter in series here, splicing at its own rate; a single shifter on the product of the two ratios is what a table-driven design would more likely do, and no value this renderer holds can be keyed on two bytes.
What either pitch byte does outside its printed range. Settings there have no state and are not drawn.
L.Bal's curve. It is drawn as the balance byte's two ramps because the page prints the two alike; only its two ends were heard, as one shifter alone each.
How the inputs are summed onto the shifters: half of each here; no reading fixed it.
The node's crossfade spans the whole half-sweep, so at small shifts it is seconds long. Whether the unit fades over a fixed share of the window instead is not asked by any candidate here.
Anything at the addresses the page does not print: no node reads them, so every candidate renders them as the power-on state.
